sources.scope: RSC/Nuffield authored Procedure and test table: separate small aliquots; nitric acid before silver nitrate; barium chloride with dilute hydrochloric acid; characteristic coloured hydroxides; known-ion flame colours and contamination notes. Its appended exam-board Specification is not used as NESA authority. Direct page/PDF open returned HTTP 405; the official indexed authored procedure was readable and checked.

RSC authored discussion links carbonate/hydrogencarbonate acid testing to the hydrochloric-acid condition for subsequent barium chloride; asks about flame-test insufficiency and damp red litmus in the ammonia test. Supports explicit carbonate/hydrogencarbonate ambiguity and supervised test framing. Official indexed authored text checked; direct open returned HTTP 405.

Authored CCI Notes 4/5 by Lyndsie Selwyn: chloride procedure, blank, known comparison solutions, contamination precautions and nitric-acid suppression of carbonate/phosphate/hydroxide interference. Detection limits and calibrated semiquantitative comparisons disprove the old absolute claim that qualitative observations can never bear on concentration. No numerical detection limit, acid concentration or conservation recipe is transferred to this lesson.

Official primary qualitative-analysis notes, printed pp15-16: calcium gives a white NaOH precipitate insoluble in excess; Cu/Fe hydroxide patterns, acidified halide tests, ammonia damp-red-litmus and CO₂ limewater response. Calcium is a counterexample to unique Mg²⁺ identification. Used for chemical observations only, never as NSW curriculum or HSC marking evidence.

RSC/Nuffield authored teaching notes distinguish barium sulfate persisting in dilute hydrochloric acid from carbonate acid reaction and confirm CO₂ via limewater; procedure notes sodium masking potassium. This does not establish all unknown white solids as sulfate or carbonate. Official indexed authored text checked.

RSC authored Results qualify observable flame colours, including copper blue/green variation and sodium masking; associated student sheet discusses atomic emission. Diagram/narration use excited species rather than claiming solution cations are necessarily the emitters. Official indexed text checked.

RSC authored Flame tests using metal salts student sheet connects heating, light emission and atoms. Only the general emission explanation is used, without claiming all flames or all elements have a unique visible colour. Official indexed text checked.

UC San Diego institutional Environmental Health and Safety guidance says not to smell chemicals for identification. Supports the lesson no-direct-smelling boundary and supervised approved procedures, not a laboratory risk assessment.

publishedReferences.text: Inquiry question: How are the ions present in the environment identified and measured?
conduct qualitative investigations – using flame tests, precipitation and complexation reactions as appropriate – to test for the presence in aqueous solution of the following ions:
cations: barium (Ba2+), calcium (Ca2+), magnesium (Mg2+), lead(II) (Pb2+), silver ion (Ag+), copper(II) (Cu2+), iron(II) (Fe2+), iron(III) (Fe3+)
anions: chloride (Cl–), bromide (Br–), iodide (I–), hydroxide (OH–), acetate (CH3COO–), carbonate (CO32–), sulfate (SO42–), phosphate (PO43–)

curriculum.scope: The 2017 mandatory hierarchy is p1287 with its p1288 cation and p1289 anion lists; flame tests, precipitation and complexation are used as appropriate. No individual named test is prescribed by this wording, and this selected-examples lesson does not certify full list coverage or a completed practical. NH₄⁺, Li⁺, Na⁺ and K⁺ are supplementary here. The former second mapping line about precipitation/net ionic equations is instructional wording, not a published syllabus quotation. Existing 2017 version, module, inquiry question and outcome IDs remain the context; no 2025 remapping or HSC mark entitlement is certified.

syllabusDotPoints: conduct qualitative investigations using flame tests, precipitation and complexation reactions to test for the presence of ions in aqueous solution
use precipitation and net ionic equations to identify ions present in a sample

inferenceDesign.workedExample: Author-created bounded model: exactly one cation from Cu²⁺/Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ and one anion from Cl⁻/Br⁻/NO₃⁻, no other interference, separate aliquots, satisfactory blank and known controls. This supplies assumptions absent from the original question rather than attributing them to NESA.
inferenceDesign.quickCheck: Original observations retained as an underdetermination problem. Calcium is a counterexample to unique magnesium identification; unacidified barium reagent does not exclude carbonate. The sulfate equation is explicitly conditional and the cation remains unresolved.
inferenceDesign.reagentContamination: HCl and BaCl₂ introduce Cl⁻; sulfuric acid introduces sulfate. Fresh aliquots and appropriate acid selection avoid identifying an ion that the analyst introduced. These conclusions follow from reagent composition and the precipitation equations.
inferenceDesign.scopeBoundary: Conceptual explanation only. Reagent concentrations, heating instructions and waste handling must come from the teacher-approved supervised procedure and risk assessment. No smell-based gas identification or unlabelled-powder testing is instructed.

requiredLabelRepairs: Show known-ion examples, fresh aliquots and controlled conditions.
Chloride: dilute HNO₃ before AgNO₃. Sulfate: dilute HCl then BaCl₂; no sulfate-containing acid.
Carbonate gas needs CO₂ confirmation. NH₃ evidence is damp red litmus turning blue; no direct smelling.
CaCO₃ white solid is not unique to calcium.
Scope the BaSO₄/BaCO₃ comparison to dilute HCl.
Combined copper observations support an inference rather than proving a unique unknown; replace equals-sign implication.
Flame emitters: excited species. Sodium can mask weaker colours.
